questions.stem: Which cookie attribute prevents `document.cookie` from reading it in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from the DOM API, which mitigates most XSS-based token theft.

questions.stem: SameSite=Lax means the cookie is sent:
choices: On top-level navigations from other sites (e.g. clicking a link) but not on cross-site subresource requests or POSTs
questions.explanation: Lax is the modern default: top-level GET navigations get the cookie; cross-site POSTs and embedded resources do not.

questions.stem: A JWT consists of:
choices: Three base64url segments: header, payload, signature
questions.explanation: JWT format is base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature). Signature lets servers verify integrity without DB lookup.

questions.stem: Which is the biggest downside of JWT vs server-side sessions?
choices: Hard to revoke before expiration without extra infrastructure
questions.explanation: JWTs are self-contained and valid until exp. Forcing logout requires a server-side blocklist, defeating the stateless advantage.

questions.stem: Putting a JWT in localStorage exposes it to:
questions.explanation: localStorage is readable by any JS on the page. An XSS payload can exfiltrate the token. It is immune to CSRF because the browser doesn't auto-send it.

questions.stem: Which scenario is a textbook CSRF attack?
choices: An attacker injects <script> via a search field
An attacker's site causes the victim's browser to POST /transfer to the victim's bank while authenticated
An attacker reads cookies via XSS
questions.explanation: CSRF rides on the auto-sent cookie. The victim is authenticated; the attacker site forges the request.

questions.stem: Which defense alone is sufficient against most CSRF in 2026 browsers?
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax blocks cross-site cookie sending on state-changing methods. Many apps add CSRF tokens as defense-in-depth.

questions.stem: In MVC, the controller is responsible for:
choices: Receiving the request, orchestrating models and views, returning the response
questions.explanation: Controllers are the glue. Models hold data/business logic, views render output, controllers orchestrate.

questions.stem: An app uses cookie sessions and needs to scale horizontally across 5 servers. What is required?
choices: A shared session store (e.g. Redis) or sticky sessions
questions.explanation: Sessions are stateful. Either every server reads from the same store, or load balancing pins each user to a server (sticky sessions).

questions.stem: Why is Secure essential for a session cookie?
choices: It encrypts the cookie at rest
It tells the browser to only send the cookie over HTTPS, preventing leakage over plain HTTP
It binds the cookie to one user
questions.explanation: Secure prevents the cookie being attached to http:// requests where a network attacker could observe it.

questions.stem: What does the JWT signature prove?
choices: That the payload was created by someone with the secret and has not been modified since
questions.explanation: HMAC/RSA over header+payload ensures integrity and authentic origin if the secret/private key was used.

questions.stem: Which is the recommended modern auth setup for browser apps?
choices: Short-lived access token + refresh token, with the refresh stored as HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Strict cookie
questions.explanation: This pattern minimises XSS exposure (refresh inaccessible to JS) and CSRF (SameSite=Strict) while keeping the access path stateless.

questions.stem: What does `req.session` come from in Express?
choices: express-session middleware that reads/writes a session store keyed by a cookie session id
questions.explanation: express-session provides the abstraction: cookie carries the id, store holds the data, req.session is the proxy object.

questions.stem: Synchronizer CSRF token defense works because:
choices: Cross-origin attackers cannot read the page to extract the token they need to include in their forged request
questions.explanation: Same-Origin Policy stops evil.com from reading bank.com's HTML to extract the token, so the forged request lacks the required token.

questions.stem: Which DELETE /users/:id status code is best when the user did not exist?
questions.explanation: 404 is correct — the resource isn't there. 204 is for a successful delete with no body.

questions.stem: Stateful (server-session) auth is preferable when:
choices: You run thousands of stateless microservices
You don't have any backend storage
questions.explanation: Deleting the session record kills access instantly across all servers reading the store.

questions.stem: What's the purpose of separating routes/ and controllers/ files?
choices: Routes wire verbs+paths to controllers; separation makes paths discoverable and controllers reusable/testable
questions.explanation: The split lets you find every endpoint in one place and unit-test controllers without spinning up an HTTP server.

questions.stem: Which HTTP method is appropriate for logging out?
questions.explanation: Logout is a state change. POST avoids GET prefetching/CSRF-via-image issues. DELETE /session is also acceptable RESTfully.

questions.stem: An attacker steals the JWT signing secret. What is the impact?
choices: They can read all data in transit
They can mint valid tokens for any user identity
Nothing — they need the user's password too
Only the next token is compromised
questions.explanation: HMAC secrets are symmetric: holder can sign arbitrary tokens. Rotate the secret immediately, invalidating all outstanding tokens.

questions.stem: Why call `req.session.regenerate()` after login?
choices: To rotate the session id, preventing session-fixation attacks
questions.explanation: If an attacker pre-set the victim's session id via fixation, regeneration after privilege change defeats them.

questions.stem: Which is true about cookies and CORS?
choices: Cookies are automatically sent on all cross-origin fetches
Cross-origin fetch sends cookies only if credentials: 'include' is set AND the server allows Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
questions.explanation: Cross-origin fetches omit cookies by default. Both client opt-in and server allow header are required.

questions.stem: The double-submit cookie pattern places the CSRF token in:
choices: Both a cookie and a request header/field; server checks they match
questions.explanation: Attackers can't read the cookie value cross-origin, so they can't replicate it in a header — match check defends without server state.

questions.stem: Why test controllers separately from routes?
choices: Routes have no logic; controllers contain decisions worth covering with unit tests
questions.explanation: Controllers carry validation, branching, and orchestration. Routes are wiring. Test the brains, not the wires.

questions.stem: An app sets Set-Cookie: sid=abc; (no attributes). Why is this insecure?
choices: Missing Secure (sent over HTTP), HttpOnly (readable by JS), and SameSite (default may vary) — leaves all common attack paths open
questions.explanation: Production session cookies should always be HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite-restricted at minimum.

questions.stem: In a JWT, where should the user role/permissions live?
questions.explanation: The payload (claims set) carries data like sub, role, exp. Header carries algorithm metadata; signature is opaque cryptographic output.
